Abstract
Background  Women´s index pregnancy emotional fertility intention was measured by asking the pregnant women 
how they would felt when they learned about their index pregnancy. Emotional health and couples´ communication 
are key during pregnancy and child birth with simultaneous minimization of reproductive coercion. Emotional fertility 
intention is critical for healthy and spaced pregnancies, as well as for better maternal and newborns outcomes. 
Besides, intentions to conceive and emotional fertility intention on pregnancy are the integral parts of women 
reproductive health (RH) right and can be considered as women decision-making ability over their fertility. Moreover, 
in low and middle-income countries including Ethiopia where the sole male´s dominance is culturally accepted 
and socially constructed, males take the lead in each decision making process including household-level decision, 
determining the family´s fertility and reproductive health service use. This dominance interferes with women fertility 
intention and their health status including their emotional feeling towards conception. In such a scenario, women 
are less likely for their say to be heard. Hence, this study aimed to determine pregnant women index pregnancy 
emotional fertility intention and to identify the associated covariates contributing to it in Ethiopia. This is a very critical 
step to generate and make actionable evidence available for the health ministry and relevant partners working on 
reproductive and women´s psycho-social health. This evidence could serve as an action point to empower women 
regarding their reproductive health right and the control over their fertility.
Methods  Nationally representative cross sectional baseline data from the Ethiopian performance monitoring for 
action (Ethiopian PMA) cohort one survey, which enrolled and collected data from currently pregnant and 6 weeks 
postpartum women were used for this study. This study collected real time data on various sexual, reproductive, 
maternal and new born nationwide priority indicators using customized Open Data Kit Mobile application. These data

Result  The overall proportion of index pregnancy emotional fertility intention of being happy was found to be 
67.81%: (95%CI: 65.38, 70.13). The proportion of pregnant women who felt very unhappy was 8% (95%CI: 6.64, 9.5)

Conclusion  The finding that 2/3 of the pregnant women felt happier calls us up to work on intended and spaced 
pregnancies by ensuring women reproductive and economic empowerment. Region specific and age sensitive 
activities and efforts that promote intended pregnancy, empower women economically; increase women´s 
enrollment to secondary education or above and assisting them in identifying their desired birth attendant as part of 
birth preparedness and complication readiness are hoped to enhance pregnant women index pregnancy emotional 
fertility intentions. Empowering women economically and improving women educational enrollment were found 
very critical to address women emotional fertility intention. Installing inter pregnancy preconception care packages 
in the health care system and postpartum contraceptive counseling’s and provision were found to be the main 
implications of the study´s findings.

Furthermore, a set of societal and individual level fac­
tors were found to influence fertility desire. At the soci­
etal level, the desire for fertility is often driven by social 
and cultural influences and the need to maintain stabil­
ity society [26, 27]. This includes strong cultural prefer­
ences for large families [26, 28] and the sex preference 
for boys over girls [29–32]. This cultural and social ele­
ment, along with sex preference, precipitated the emo­
tional aspect of fertility intention. Besides, the current 
situation of social unrest and volatile politics including 
internally displaced people; the cross boarder migration 
owing to the conflicts and the economic crisis across the 
globe are the macro level factors which are further pre­
cipitating women emotional well-being and their mental 
health [33–36]. At the individual level, characteristics 
such as age [37, 38], number of living children [39, 40], 
marital status, wealth, education level [41–45], place of 
residence [46–48], husband emotional fertility intention 
[49] and socio-demographic characteristics of the women 
[41, 42] are associated with fertility desire. Although 
numerous factors have been shown to influence fertility 
desire, there is a relative dearth of literature on emotional 
fertility intention in Ethiopia where the desire for addi­
tional child is pronounced [41, 50]. Moreover, there is a 
dearth of evidence on women’s emotional fertility inten­
tions, such as what pregnant women would have felt 
when learned about their index pregnancy [2]. Hence, 
determining the degree to which women experience of 
additional pregnancy and identifying its correlates which 
contribute for such variation among currently pregnant 
women thereby reducing maternal mortality and improv­
ing newborns outcomes is very imperative. Therefore, the 
aim of this study was to quantify the magnitude of index 
pregnancy emotional fertility intention and to identify 
factors associated with through further analysis of the 
national women and newborns baseline survey data of 
the Ethiopian Performance monitoring for action (ETH-
PMA) cohort one study.
Methods and data sources
Study design and population and sample size
The Ethiopian Performance Monitoring for Action (Eth-
PMA) cohort one cross sectional data from the baseline 
survey were used for this study [51]. All pregnant women 
with gestational age of 1 to 9 months at the time of and 
those within less than six weeks postpartum during the 
screening and enrollment phase were screed using the 
female screening form prepared for identifying eligible 
women. This was followed by administrating the female 
baseline questionnaire. In the female baseline question­
naire women were asked about their antenatal care 
sought thus far during their index pregnancy, partner 
support and perceived community encouragement on the 
use the three main domains of the maternal and newborn 
care continuum components; their reproductive and 
sexual history, their birth preparedness and complication 
readiness; about their agreement and disagreement on 
girls and women empowerment towards contraceptive 
use and women sexual and reproductive issues; about 
their contraceptive use history and their current and 
future fertility intention.
Most important to this study was that women were 
asked how they did they felt when learned about their 
index pregnancy. This variable was regarded as index 
pregnancy emotional fertility intentions which is the 
main outcome variable of this study. This study was 
restricted to pregnant women by enrollment and a total 
of 2236 pregnant women were included in this further 
analysis. The overall sample size and cell sample size 
adequacy was checked and found to be adequate to gen­
erating unbiased estimates on index pregnancy emo­
tional fertility intention when learned about their index 
pregnancy.
Data collection and field work
Cohort one baseline cross-sectional data were collected 
from Nov 2019 to Jan 2020. The details of the field work 
implementation were reported elsewhere [51]. The first 
field work of the panel baseline survey was screening 
pregnant women and those who were in their less than 
six weeks post-partum. A two - stage stratified cluster 
sampling method was used to select enumeration areas. 
Complete census was conducted in the selected enumer­
ation areas to recruit and enroll current pregnant women 
and women who were less than 6 weeks post-partum. 
It was executed by Addis Ababa University’s School of 
Public Health in collaborative efforts with the Ethiopian 
Public Health Association with assistance from the Fed­
eral Health Minister, Central Statistical Services, Bill &

In order to maximize the sample of pregnant women; a 
census of all the panel enumeration areas (EAs) was con­
ducted and eligible women were screened and enrolled to 
the study. In order not to miss all pregnant and six week 
postpartum women by then in the selected enumera­
tions areas (EAs), complete census of pregnant and those 
women in their six weeks postpartum was conducted in 
the selected enumeration areas. All women aged 15–49 
who were usual members of the household were screened 
by using self-reported current pregnancy status assess­
ment question and approximate gestational age embed­
ded in the screening questionnaire. If they were found 
to be pregnant or in their six weeks postpartum period, 
they were approached for enrollment in the panel study 
and women who have been voluntarily consented were 
recruited to participate in the follow up study. For the 
census, a 95% response rate was assumed, that the aver­
age number of women aged 15–49 per household is 0.98, 
and of these, 10% have reported of being pregnant or 42 
days postpartum– the calculated sample size was found 
to be sufficient to examine selected key maternal and 
newborn health (MNH) indicators at the national level 
with 5% margin of error. The survey was not anticipated 
to provide representatives estimates of all maternal and 
newborn care indicators at the regional level. The main 
sample units or enumeration areas (EAs) were chosen 
using the frame from the Ethiopia Population and Hous­
ing Census (PHC), which was conducted in 2019 by the 
Ethiopia Central Statistical Services. Of the total 265 
EAs which were chosen in the first stage with indepen­
dent selection in each sampling stratum and a probabil­
ity proportional to EA size; pregnant women from 217 
EAs which were selected from the six panel regions were 
included in this further analysis. In second stage, a census 
of all households was conducted in all the selected EAs 
to obtain adequate sample size of pregnant and six weeks 
postpartum women and to improve the study´s power. 
The protocol of PMA Ethiopia contains all the details on 
sample design and selection probabilities, design effects 
and sampling methods [51].
 Variables
 Outcome variable
The main outcome variable was Index pregnancy emo­
tional fertility intention among currently pregnant 
women. It was measured by a likert scale question with 5 
scales as shown in the annexed supplementary file. Cur­
rently pregnant women were asked as follows: when you 
found out you were pregnant how did you feel? For the 
seek of getting a meaning out this specific scale of mea­
surement, the scale was reverse coded so that the very 
happy category gets the larger value on the scale and the 
very unhappy labeled as the smallest value across the 
scale. Since the outcome variable has more than two cat­
egories unlike the binary category, multinomial logistics 
regression was used [51].
 Independent variables
Independent variables were classified into individual-
level variables and enumeration area-level variables. 
Individual-level independent variables further cat­
egorized into socio-demographic characteristics, parity 
and other reproductive health characteristics, “Region” 
was grouped into six categories: 1 = Afar, 2 = Tigray 
3 = Amhara, 4 = Oromia, 7 = SNNPRs and 10 = Addis 
Ababa city administration. Place of residence follows the 
default urban/rural classification.

Analysis and measurement
The panel baseline cross-sectional data set for cohort 
one survey were used for this analysis. Data were ana­
lyzed using STATA v16: Copyright 1985–2019 StataCorp 
LLC Statistics/Data Analysis StataCorp 4905 Lakeway 
Drive, Special Edition College Station, Texas 77,845 USA, 
800-STATA-PC https://www.stata.com, 979–696–4600 
http://www.stata@stata.com, 979–696–4601(fax). This 
analysis used a single-user Stata perpetual license with 
Serial number: 401606348636). Frequencies and percent­
ages were computed to characterize the study popula­
tion. Chi-square test statistics were computed to check 
cell sample size adequacy and the sample size was found 
to be adequate to provide unbiased estimates.
Exploratory data analysis were conducted for data 
cleaning, which involved checking item nonresponse rate 
for each variable and don’t know response which were 
later excluded from the analysis. Following this variable 
were recoded to create empirically plausible categories, 
and the distribution of the recoded variables was checked 
using mean and proportion.
Given the outcome variable has more than two cat­
egories; we have preferred to fit multinomial logistic 
regression modeling over the traditional binary logistics 
regression [52]. Multinomial logistics regression model­
ing was fitted to identify important predictor variables 
for pregnant women emotional fertility intention when 
learned about their index pregnancy. A p value cut of 0.25 
was used to select candidate variables for multinomial 
multivariate logistics regression model fitting. Results 
were presented in the form of percentage, and odds ratio 
with 95% CI. Statistical significance was declared at a p 
value of 0.05.
Model fitness test was checked using the command 
«mlogitgof» and the result revealed that the model was 
fit. This implied that variables included in the final multi­
nomial logistics regression model which are the systemic 
components of the model fitting process that explained 
the observed variation in pregnant women index preg­
nancy emotional fertility intention. This is supported by 
the model fitness test result with a chi-squared statis­
tic = 17.057 and degrees of freedom = 16.
Data quality management and control
Data completeness for variables and items for generat­
ing composite variables was checked by exploratory data 
analysis after which any item nonresponse was excluded 
from the analysis. Frequencies were run to exclude non 
knowledge assessing responses with do not know (DNK) 
and no response (NR).
The Ethiopian PMA survey used a standard and pre­
tested tools. Besides, providing rigorous ToT for regional 
coordinators and supervisors, hands-on training using 
small group modality with mock interviews among resi­
dent enumerators, pretesting the tool, close supervisor 
during filed work, real time progress report and error 
correction response, 10% random check were some of the 
modalities used to maintain the quality of the collected 
data, the detail was reported somewhere else [51].
Ethical consideration
This study involved a secondary analysis of deidenti­
fied data from the PMA Ethiopia. The PMA Ethiopia 
survey was conducted after obtaining ethical approval 
from Bloomberg School of Public Health at Johns Hop­
kins University in Baltimore, USA and Addis Ababa 
University. Informed consent was obtained from respon­
dents during the data collection process of PMA Ethio­
pia on the baseline data collection from Oct 2019 to Jan 
2020. Minors less than 15 years as per the law were not 
included in this study. Informed verbal consent was take 
from study participants.
Result
Magnitude of pregnant women emotional fertility 
intention about their index pregnancy: evidence from ETH-
PMA cohort one baseline survey, n = 2,236
The overall proportion of index pregnancy emotional 
fertility intention of being happy was found to be 67.81% 
95% CI: 65.38%, 70.13%. More specifically, 41.88% 
(95%CI: 39.47%, 43.33% felt very happy and 25.92% 
(95%CI: 23.83%, 28.13%) of them reported that they felt a 
sort of happy when they learned about their index preg­
nancy. Besides, the proportion of pregnant women index 
pregnancy emotional fertility intention of being very 
unhappy was found to be 8% (95%CI: 6.64%, 9.5%) while 
8.45% (95%CI: 7.13%, 10.0%) and 15.79% (95%CI: 14.01%, 
17.76%) of the pregnant women have self-reported that 
they have felt a sort of unhappy and mixed feelings 
respectively when they learned about their index preg­
nancy (Fig. 1).

The proportion of pregnant women index pregnancy 
emotional fertility intentions of being of very unhappy, a 
sort of unhappy, mixed feelings, a sort of happy and very 
happy when the pregnant women learned about their 
index pregnancy was 9.54%, 11.12%, 18.01%, 30.29% and

In addition, the proportion of emotional fertility inten­
tion varied by region, wealth index and by their residence. 
This proportion of pregnant women index pregnancy 
emotional fertility intention was found to be 3.68%, 
5.69%, 14.68%, 27.26% and 48.69% for the respective 
feeling categories among women residing in the house­
holds with higher wealth quintile. Similarly, for the resi­

66.04% of the pregnant women reported that they felt 
very unhappy, a sort of unhappy, mixed feelings, a sort 
of happy and very happy respectively. Besides, among 
residents of Addis Ababa, 2.77%, 4.48%, 7.80%, 32.4%

Discussion
In countries like Ethiopia where male´s dominance over 
fertility and reproductive health service use decisions has 
been culturally accepted and social constructed, investi­
gating the factors affecting the level of women emotional 
fertility intentions when they learned about their index 
pregnancy and identifying the factors contributing for 
this variation has paramount importance to build and 
sustain a healthy and economically sound family. In midst 
of the SDG period, measuring pregnant women index 
pregnancy emotional fertility intention as a measure of 
their reproductive health right and decision making over 
their reproductive health is very crucial. This could gen­
erate and provide an actionable evidence for the health 
ministry and relevant actors to enhance women decision 
making on their desired emotional fertility in particular 
and reproductive health right in general which in turn 
provides evidence to track for SDG 5.6.1.
The finding that the proportion of women emotional 
fertility intention was 67.81%: (65.38%, 70.13%) when 
they learned about their index pregnancy was higher 
than findings from studies [1, 23, 53] while lower than the 
finding from a study [5]. The relatively higher proportion 
of being happy might be related with the success story of 
health extension program (HEP) in the Ethiopia, Health 
Sector Transformational Plans I_II (HSTP 2) [18, 19], the 
millennium development goals (MGDs) success stories 
alongside with the endorsement and implementation of 
the new reproductive health strategy running through 
2021 to 25 in which preconception care packages and 
fertility related targets were included [19]. The mecha­
nism through which the government of Ethiopian Health 
Minister commitment may enhance emotional fertility 
intention is through the recent focus in the provision of 
quality service [54–56] and client centered care and pro­
vision of quality health services [55] which contributed 
for an improved client service use satisfaction.
To this end, the implication of the finding that only 
four in ten pregnant women felt very happy when they 
learned about their index pregnancy indicated that we 
have a long way to go to make women decided on their 
fertility desire including their emotional fertility readi­
ness as well as availing fertility and reproduction related 
preconception care packages which is relatively new for 
our country [21, 57, 58]. Furthermore, the expansion of 
the urban health extension professionals and addition of 
level IV health extension workers in rural areas is likely 
to enhance the quality of care [59] at the community 
level thereby enabling women to get informed counseling 
about their reproductive health needs and rights includ­
ing planning and spacing their pregnancies. Those who 
have got exposure for such care and counseling might 
have planned their desired family size and felt happy 
when learned about their index pregnancy owing to the 
fact that the indexpregnancy is likely to be intended. 
Moreover, the government’s effort to enhance the quality 
of maternal and child health care and respectful mater­
nity care [60] along with the continuum of care is likely 
to encourage women to plan their pregnancies and be 
happy when learned about their index pregnancy.
The finding that the likelihood of women emotional 
fertility intention of being happy when they learned 
about their index pregnancy was found to be higher 
among women from the well to do households might also 
be related with good couples communication [10, 61] and 
their influence in household level decision-making and 
health service use autonomy [62, 63]. This involvement 
enables women to contribute their share in controlling 
their family fertility desire and subsequently make them 
feel happy when learned about their index pregnancy. 
The possible explanations is that women residing in the 
richest households are very likely to be happy since they 
felt empowered to avail themselves of the ‘luxury’ of 
couples conversation, understanding and health service 
usage, especially in LMICs.
Similarly, the finding that elders had increased like­
lihood of emotional fertility intention of being happy 
when they have learned about their index pregnancy is 
likely emanated from their previous pregnancy and child 
bearing experiences [64] leading them well prepared for 
their index pregnancies and might also be resulted from 
improved spousal communication [10, 65].
The finding women intended to have another child 
increased the likelihood of the pregnant women

emotional fertility intention of being happy when they 
learned about their index pregnancy is related with the 
families’ aspiration to achieve the desired family size and 
can be seen as exercising women reproductive right and 
reproductive autonomy [66]. Moreover, the finding that 
the likelihood of pregnant women who felt happy when 
they learned about their index pregnancy was lower 
among those with higher birth order and those who do 
not want any more child might be related with women 
prior adverse pregnancy experience [64]. It is likely to 
be related with males decision making on the number of 
children forcing them to became pregnant [7, 63, 67]. In 
addition, the finding that higher birth order lower preg­
nant women likelihood of being happy when learned 
about their index pregnancy is in line with the findings 
from on women fertility desire studies [41, 68]. The find­
ing that lower likelihood of index pregnancy emotional 
fertility intentions of being happy when they have learned 
their index pregnancy in the two regions; namely the for­
mer Southern Nations, Nationalities and People Region 
and Oromiya regions was found to be not in line with [5, 
42]. While a study among non-pregnant women based 
of cross sectional data from performance monitoring 
for action Ethiopia revealed no association statistical 
between region and women emotional fertility intention 
[1].
The finding that women attending primary education 
and those who desired birth attendant is family member 
had reduced pregnant women mixed feelings when the 
pregnant women learned about their pregnancy might 
be related with, that those educated [69] have the knowl­
edge and awareness as well as they could exercise their 
reproductive autonomy and able to decide on the tim­
ing and number of pregnancies [70, 71]. Besides, access 
and care for modern health service and qualified health 
professionals as the government´s commitment to assure 
health service provision at high quality standard [19] and 
among other service reproductive, maternal and new 
born health care service are at the core [21]. The finding 
that not attending better education lowered the likeli­
hood of mixed emotional feelings is in line with findings 
from studies on fertility desire studies [41, 72].
This study is not spared of limitations. To start with, the 
reliance on self-reported history data to measure index 
pregnancy emotional fertility intention might introduce 
potential bias. This might be coupled with some sort 
of social desirability bias since women are less likely in 
speaking negatively about their pregnancy since this is 
a communal event and socially and culturally sensitive 
reproductive health issue in Ethiopia. However, such 
findings offer meaningful insights in measuring index 
pregnancy emotional fertility intention. Besides, further 
research is needed to validate and build upon these ini­
tial results. In addition, the Ethiopian PMA cohort one 
baseline data didn’t collect information on variables such 
as husband desired number of children, husband employ­
ment and women employment and most importantly 
household-level decision making and attitude that sur­
round the emotional aspect of fertility intention in rela­
tion to cultural aspect were not measured in this study.
Conclusion
The finding that 2/3 of the women felt happier calling up 
on intended and spaced pregnancies by ensuring women 
reproductive health service use autonomy and economic 
empowerment as well as improving women education 
enrollment. The fact that 1/3 felt mixed emotions and 
unhappy feelings also calls to further enhance women 
decision over their fertility and their reproductive health 
right.
Region specific and age sensitive activities and efforts 
that promote intended pregnancies, empowering women 
economically are hoped to enhance women index preg­
nancy emotional fertility intention of being happier while 
promoting secondary education or above and being pre­
pared in identifying their desired birth attendant as part 
the birth preparedness and complication readiness plan 
are hoped to improve index pregnancy emotional fertil­
ity intention of mixed feelings about their index preg­
nancy. In addition, future further analysis may consider 
ordered logistics regression analysis though the use of 
multinomial regression is possible. Moreover, future 
surveys need to collect data on variables related cultural 
aspect that affect women emotional fertility intention in 
terms of women attitude alongside with husband desired 
number of children, husband employment and women 
employment and most importantly household level deci­
sion making. Besides, additional studies are needed to 
come up with a direct measurement of index pregnancy 
emotional fertility intention including validating this 
direct measurement tool to be developed. Furthermore, 
future similar further analysis which are based on PMA-
ETH data need to consider linking the community data 
with the health facility data to control facility related 
factors.
Implication of the study
Enabling women to choose their birth attendant as part 
of their birth preparedness and complication readiness 
plan is an important implication of the study. Besides, 
installing the inter pregnancy preconception care pack­
ages in the health care system alongside with postpartum 
contraceptive counseling’s and actual service provision 
were found to be the main implications of the study find­
ings. Empowering women economically and improving 
women educational enrollment is another implication 
of the study. Furthermore, region specific and culturally

Abstract: Background Women´s index pregnancy emotional fertility intention was measured by asking the pregnant women how they would felt when they learned about their index pregnancy. Emotional health and couples´ communication are key during pregnancy and child birth with simultaneous minimization of reproductive coercion. Emotional fertility intention is critical for healthy and spaced pregnancies, as well as for better maternal and newborns outcomes. Besides, intentions to conceive and emotional fertility intention on pregnancy are the integral parts of women reproductive health (RH) right and can be considered as women decision-making ability over their fertility. Moreover, in low and middle-income countries including Ethiopia where the sole male´s dominance is culturally accepted and socially constructed, males take the lead in each decision making process including household-level decision, determining the family´s fertility and reproductive health service use. This dominance interferes with women fertility intention and their health status including their emotional feeling towards conception. In such a scenario, women are less likely for their say to be heard. Hence, this study aimed to determine pregnant women index pregnancy emotional fertility intention and to identify the associated covariates contributing to it in Ethiopia. This is a very critical step to generate and make actionable evidence available for the health ministry and relevant partners working on reproductive and women´s psycho-social health. This evidence could serve as an action point to empower women regarding their reproductive health right and the control over their fertility. Methods Nationally representative cross sectional baseline data from the Ethiopian performance monitoring for action (Ethiopian PMA) cohort one survey, which enrolled and collected data from currently pregnant and 6 weeks postpartum women were used for this study. This study collected real time data on various sexual, reproductive, maternal and new born nationwide priority indicators using customized Open Data Kit Mobile application. These data were collected using standard pretested questionnaire prepared in English and the three local languages (Amharic, Afan Oromo and Tigrigna) by well experienced resident enumerators.
